en: Who had been a friend of David,
A man of sacred power,
A khan of treasures,
The smith Bolokbai was there too.
Tekechi's Ormonbek—
When all the khans had gathered,
The bold son born of Manas
Had these words to say:
“Almambet's son Kulchoro,
My kinsman like a twin lamb,
Has reached twelve years of age.
For this very one's wish
I have prayed to God.
My flag fixed upon a spear,
My father's friend Almambet
Saying, “Let him take him as support,”
Left as a gift for me.
This Kulchoro standing here—
That his heart might be fat,
I had a young mare slaughtered,
And fed him his fill of its belly fat.
When he was six, I took him,
Had an amulet hung about his neck,
And among the Argyn and Kyrgyz
Had him raised with loving care.
I let him wear no dirty shirt,
Nor drink from a dirty bowl.
I took the child as my protector,
Since childhood,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro
I had suckled in equal shares.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
My poplars set before me for protection,
From Almambet and Chubak
The charge I inherited.
My protective otter at my collar,
The bright star above your head.
Kicking one another like young colts,
‘Let their name be something special,’
My sorrowful mother Kanykei said.
To make them true kin,
She suckled them with milk from her white breasts.
They shared the same delights;
Semetey and these boys
Lay upon one bed.
Our blood is one, our souls separate.
Impartial khans, hear me!
Kulchoro is twelve,
Kanchoro is fourteen.
No idea in China
These are noble at their roots,
Children of princes.
Semetey, his father's only son,
Has taken these two as his support.
At sight of them my longing is eased.
If hardship falls upon my troubled head,
Through whom I shall inflict grievous torment.
You have raised uproar in the land;
Khans gathered in your ranks, hear me:
My tail feathers have matured.
When its wings have grown to match,
Would a falcon stand unready?
God has understood my wish.
When the days are counted,
When the days are set in writing,
The weapon at my side,
This Kulchoro standing here,
Has reached twelve years this year.
My Kanchoro, whom I take as support,
Has reached fourteen years.
With leopard Bakai at your head,
Impartial khans, look here!
Can a prince's son,
Without seeking news of the Chinese,
Simply stand and watch?
A nobleman's only son—
Listen to the orphan.
Can he lie without a care,
Once his stride has reached its strength,
Without breaking ranks in spear combat,
Without falling to a bullet if his time has come,
In paradisal Great Beijing
Without fighting in the tumult?
Can one become a man without doing so?
One of the seven days is death;
Can one who fears death prosper?
The Chinese with their sovereign, the khagan's people—
Can we refrain from fighting them?
With the Chin khagan and Machin,
Can a man remain without a quarrel?
If we simply lie in one place,
Will God not strike us down?
Dark as a cloud of mist,
People of Kakan-Chyn;
With my father Khan Manas at their head,
Ask no more of the twelve heroes,
Against the true Chinese in Beijing,
May we die if we do not fight!
‘I was born of a father as a man’—
Better that we had never been born!
This year against the mottled-bearded Manchu
Let us openly wage a holy war.
Against the unbelievers like black worms,
Let us charge with level spears!
The Argyn and Kyrgyz are brothers.
Shygai's son Chynkozho
Let us fasten at our waist as support.
If Chynkozho agrees to my plan,
I shall gird my waist firmly.
From Kongurbai in Beijing
I shall exact my father's blood-price.
Upon the unbelievers like black worms
I shall bring devastation.
From that dog, not for one father alone,
But for forty fathers I shall take revenge.
Uncle Bakai, Ormonbek,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You four go and return.
Shygai's son Chynkozho,
A khoja capable in all he does,
Who dwells at Kebez-Too,
A hero said to be stately,
Who wears a black flower-patterned coat,
Who rides a black racehorse,
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
Was one of the discerning heroes.
That bold man, built like an elephant,
Is the support to fasten at our waist.
Against the khagan's Beijing,
If we should come to blows,
He is the hero who will show courage.
If we firmly level our spears,
Fire guns and draw bows,
And fight with crashing blows,
He will stand beneath the standard,
And slaughter the Chinese.
If an evil day comes and blood flows,
If a day of terrible hardship dawns,
He will stand without flinching,
And show courage to the full.
He is the support to fasten at our waist,
The hero who will go to Beijing.
Uncle Bakai, you four,
Bring that man here!
Chynkozho and I
Were strongmen joined in strength,
Heroes joined at heart.
If I follow the old accounts,
If I ask those who know,
When the dark gun crashes,
He is a hero who does not flee.
When the fierce gun cracks,
He is one who feels no fear.
Before, when my bloodthirsty father lived,
Lest the people fall into disorder,
Dwelling at broad Sary-Kol,
Among the people known as Oigut,
Akbaltai, khan of the Oigut,
Had asked for hostages and received them.
Shygai and Chynkozho,
By the command of God,
Had remained at Kebez-Too.
That was the reason these kinsmen
Had become separated.
Thus Chynkozho,
After his father Shygai died,
Had grown distant.
When from Temir Khan's city
I wandered here and settled,
He made no joyful feast,
Slaughtered no welcoming sheep.
‘My orphan younger kinsman has come’—
He did not even show his face,
Nor offer food to gladden me.
Before, when my gray-maned father died,
When the people gathered and buried him,
Not one came to offer prayers.
My grieving mother Kanykei—
Not one came to see her.
On slopes across from one another,
Let him ponder these words of mine:
We share one root and one nest.
If Chynkozho joins us in unity,
If he settles along Ken-Kol,
And I settle along broad Talas,
If we bring our wisdom together,
If we stir six clusters of stars in heaven,
If we become friends unto the next world,
If the two of us become one,
Could any fingered man prevail against us?
Could any nail-bearing person attack us?
Will they not advance upon us one day?
Could Khan Kongurbai attack us?
If we are kin to the khoja,
Present six swift horses,
And promptly offer wealth without stint.
Bring Chynkozho here,
To the orphan, his father's only son.
Uncle Bakai, you leopard,
Make him my companion!
Our fathers are equal kin;
We are brothers of a single root.
Covering the children,
Have him move his camp here.
If he does not agree to my words,
‘The tribute owed to my father,
Counting the years exactly,
Pay it now,’ tell him.
Bring this stern demand upon him!
If he will not heed you,
Tell Chubak's son Kanchoro
To raise an uproar.
Tell Almambet's Kulchoro
To raid and take his horses.
If he will not accept your plan,
If he will not heed your words,
Tell him, ‘May your sworn oath strike you down!
Without appearing before my eyes,
Let him become my enemy!’”
Earnestly pleading for this,
He gave six swift horses,
And a letter the size of a palm.
His heart burning, he turned about,
And sent the four impartial men.
The young sultan, the gray-maned hero,
Displayed his princely rank.
Upon Abyke's Aktelki
He mounted Kulchoro;
Upon Khan Kobosh's Kokteke
He mounted Kanchoro.
Those four impartial men
He sent to Chynkozho.
When set at the front, a bringer of good fortune,
If you are driving, please support
Traveling along the mountain tops,
He roamed the face of the land,
Crossing hill after hill,
Crossing mottled, ridged passes,
The hero Bakai, the leopard,
Along the ridge stretching across,
Along the clear spring waters,
The hero Bakai led the way.
They crossed Maseyil,
Traveled through broad Kashgar,
Skirted great Khotan,
Wearing out their peerless steeds,
And reached Kebez-Too.
Your caravan guide, old Bakai,
Your saint with sweet words,
To the hero Kozho's royal court,
To his fortified stronghold—
Zhangyryk's Zhar-Kyya,
Above it was Kebez-Too.
A single horse could pass in file.
Shygai's son Chynkozho,
Who dwelt at Kebez-Too,
